contraindications: Hemiplegic migraine and migraine with brainstem aura: triptans are excluded by the product labels because of a theoretical vasoconstrictive risk and no trial data; avoid.
Ergot derivatives (ergotamine, dihydroergotamine): avoid in hemiplegic migraine for the same reason.
Triptans are also contraindicated by label after stroke or TIA, in ischaemic heart disease, peripheral vascular disease and uncontrolled hypertension.
interactions: Aspirin 75 mg (current): no pharmacokinetic interaction with triptans.
output.summary: Triptans and ergots are label-restricted in hemiplegic migraine; an NSAID with an antiemetic is the usual acute treatment.
warnings: A retrospective series of 76 people with hemiplegic migraine treated with triptans reported no ischaemic events (Artto V et al., Eur J Neurol 2007;14:1053-1056); the label restriction still applies.

results.finding: Hemiplegic migraine needs at least two attacks with fully reversible motor weakness and fully reversible visual, sensory and/or speech symptoms; motor symptoms may last up to 72 hours. The sporadic form has no affected first- or second-degree relative.
results.source: Headache Classification Committee of the IHS. ICHD-3. Cephalalgia 2018;38:1-211 (1.2.3 Hemiplegic migraine)

results.finding: CACNA1A, ATP1A2 and SCN1A variants explain part of familial and a minority of sporadic cases; the first attack needs exclusion of stroke and other secondary causes. Acute treatment usually relies on NSAIDs and antiemetics because vasoconstrictors are label-restricted.
results.source: Russell MB, Ducros A. Sporadic and familial hemiplegic migraine: pathophysiological mechanisms, clinical characteristics, diagnosis, and management. Lancet Neurol 2011;10:457-470

output.summary: Hemiplegic migraine is defined by repeated reversible motor aura; first attacks require exclusion of secondary causes, and acute treatment avoids vasoconstrictors by convention.

prohibited_recommendations: Do not prescribe triptans or ergot derivatives: they are avoided in hemiplegic migraine; use an NSAID with an antiemetic.

Do not start antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy for presumed TIA: the episode had the features of migraine aura (a positive sensory symptom spreading over 20-25 minutes, then motor and speech symptoms in succession, followed by a migrainous headache, on a background of typical visual aura) and imaging shows no infarct.
required_recommendations: Stop the aspirin started for possible TIA: the episode was a migraine aura with motor features, imaging shows no infarct and he has no other indication for antiplatelet therapy; explain this to the patient and his GP.

For acute attacks use an NSAID (naproxen 500 mg or ibuprofen 400-600 mg) with an antiemetic (metoclopramide 10 mg or prochlorperazine) at headache onset; avoid triptans and ergots while hemiplegic migraine is the working diagnosis.
Give a headache diary and review; start prevention if motor aura recurs (verapamil, lamotrigine, or flunarizine where licensed).
Refer to clinical genetics for hemiplegic migraine gene testing (CACNA1A, ATP1A2, SCN1A, PRRT2) if motor aura recurs or a relative is affected.
Ask his GP to assess cardiovascular risk (blood pressure, lipids, HbA1c and QRISK3, which counts migraine) and treat his hypertension if it stays above target.

avoided_actions.rationale: Head CT is less sensitive than MRI for migraine-relevant structural causes and is not indicated in typical migraine with aura; even when imaging is warranted, MRI is preferred
Lumbar puncture is not indicated in migraine with aura; reserve for suspected SAH (with normal CT) or meningitis; neither is present here

accepted: Probable sporadic hemiplegic migraine (ICHD-3 1.2.3) — first definite motor aura episode with antecedent visual aura episodes

differential.key_features: Positive symptoms spreading over 20-25 minutes, then weakness and speech change in succession, followed by migrainous headache, in a man with years of typical visual aura; MRI shows no infarct and MRA no stenosis or dissection. A normal DWI does not exclude TIA; the distinction is clinical.
No neck pain or trauma; cervical MRA shows no intimal flap or intramural haematoma.
Seizure symptoms spread over seconds; a 20-25 minute sensory march followed by weakness and a migrainous headache is aura.
No first- or second-degree relative with motor aura, which defines the sporadic form.
Father's stroke at 68 is a common late-life event; MRI shows three punctate frontal subcortical hyperintensities with normal anterior temporal white matter and external capsules.

key_clinical_evidence: Years of typical visual aura every few months, then a first attack of right hand tingling spreading over 20-25 minutes, followed by grip weakness and slurred speech, resolving in 25-30 minutes and followed by migrainous headache.
One motor attack and no affected relative: probable sporadic hemiplegic migraine; ICHD-3 needs a second motor attack for 1.2.3.
Brain MRI shows no infarct and MRA shows normal intracranial and cervical arteries; the aspirin started for possible TIA has no indication.
Triptans and ergots are label-restricted in hemiplegic migraine: acute treatment is an NSAID with an antiemetic.

patient.history_present_illness:
A 42-year-old Pakistani-British man was referred to the neurology outpatient clinic after being evaluated in the emergency department 10 days ago for what was documented as a 'possible TIA or hemiplegic migraine.' He describes a single episode in which he was at work when he developed a gradual onset tingling in his right hand that over approximately 20-25 minutes progressed to involve his right forearm, and he noticed his grip strength was reduced — he dropped his pen. He also noticed mild difficulty articulating words during the episode, saying his speech felt 'slow and thick.' The sensory and motor symptoms lasted approximately 25-30 minutes and resolved completely. Immediately afterwards, he developed a left-sided throbbing headache that built up over about 30 minutes to 9/10, far worse than his usual mild headaches, with nausea, severe photophobia, and phonophobia. He vomited three times. The headache lasted 18 hours.

He had no prior episodes of this type. However, on careful questioning, he says he had 'visual episodes' once every few months over the past 4-5 years — brief shimmering lights in one corner of his vision, lasting 15-20 minutes, after which he had a mild headache that he attributed to 'eyestrain' or 'stress' and took paracetamol. He never consulted a doctor about these and had not made the connection. He has mild hypertension, is a non-smoker, and his father had a stroke at age 68. He is a secondary school science teacher. His GP started him on aspirin 75 mg after the ED visit pending specialist review.
